## Personality

Weathered, blunt and superstitious, with a ritual for everything from casting off to tying her boots. She trusts the sea more than people, and people only a little.

## Lore

Annis is seventy-six, the captain of the Saltlark, and the oldest captain on the harbour council. She is weathered, blunt and superstitious, and she has a ritual for everything, from tying her boots (left first, double knot, never on the deck) to casting off (a pinch of salt over the stern and a word to the water that nobody has ever been close enough to hear). She trusts the sea more than she trusts people, and people only a little.

### A long life on the water

Annis was born in a fisherman's cottage on the Waterfront and went to sea at ten, and she has commanded the Saltlark for forty-four years. The Saltlark is a small, deep, stubborn coasting ship, almost as old as her captain, and Annis will hear no word against her. Annis has never married and has no children. "The Saltlark is enough trouble," she says, and she means it fondly.

She remembers when the bay was as calm as a millpond. When she was young, she says, you could row out past the headland on a summer evening and hear nothing but the oars and the gulls, and the deep water was simply deep water. She does not say this as an old woman's complaint about the past. She says it as a captain giving a report.

### The water has changed

Since the Disturbance began, Annis has watched the sea change, slowly at first and then less slowly. The swells come wrong. The fish run in the wrong places. Birds she has known all her life no longer settle on the water past the headland. And on the Saltlark's last voyage, in deep water on a still night, something large brushed along her keel from bow to stern and was gone. The whole ship felt it. Annis took the Saltlark home at once, and the next morning she went to Ambrose the chartmaker and gave him the mark herself.

Her sailor Morwenna, who has crewed for her for twelve years and who is the closest thing Annis has to family, felt it too. Annis has noticed that Morwenna has not talked about it at home, and she has not pressed her.

Annis wants the harbour council to take the sea seriously before something goes wrong. She does not know what she wants it to do, exactly, and that is her trouble: every time she says so, Captain Corwin asks her what she would have them do and what it would cost. Corwin is her favourite rival on the council. They disagree on harbour dues, on loading order, on whether a ship should cast off under a new moon (it should not), and on almost everything else. She thinks he is a fine seaman and an infuriating man, and she would trust him with her ship, which she would not say about anyone else on the council.

### The old rival

Her oldest rival is Thaddeus, who now spends his days on a bench by the water. When they were young, the two of them raced each other across the bay at every chance and quarrelled over who ought to skipper the harbour's boat in the summer race around Veligor. More than thirty years ago the helm went to Thaddeus, and he lost to Goa Harbour by a boat's length. Annis has told him ever since that she would have won. Thaddeus says she would have lost by two. They have had this argument several hundred times and both of them would be lost without it.

### What she fears

Annis is not afraid of storms, or of wrecks, or of dying at sea, which she has always expected to do. She is afraid that the harbour will wait for proof until the proof is a ship that does not come home.

### Hooks

A quest could sail on the Saltlark to the place where her keel was brushed, help Annis put a case to the council that even Corwin cannot dismiss, or perform one of her rituals for her when, for the first time in forty-four years, she cannot.
